title: Now, if you want it
hookLine: all you pray to reach later, you can have now, if you stop refusing it (Meditations 12.1)

cards: Someday, when the kids are grown. Someday, when the debt is paid off. Someday, after the promotion, after the move, after the test results come back clear.
Then I'll be calm. Then I'll be kind. Then I'll really live.
Book twelve is the last book of the Meditations, and its very first entry takes apart that word, someday.

teach.h: WHAT YOU SEEK, YOU CAN HAVE NOW.
teach.b: First, the claim. All the things you hope to reach by a long, roundabout road, Marcus writes, you can have now, if you don't refuse them to yourself. Second, how.

teach.h: LEAVE THE PAST, TRUST THE FUTURE.
teach.b: Leave the past alone. Hand the future over to providence.
And set the present right, just the present, toward reverence and justice. Third, what those two words mean here.
Reverence, he says, so that you love what has been given you, since nature brought it to you, and you to it.
Justice, so that you speak the truth freely and plainly, and act according to law and to what each thing deserves.
And don't let anything stop you: not other people's badness, not their opinions, not your own body's complaints. Fourth, the sting at the end.
It isn't death you should fear, Marcus says, but never beginning to live according to nature. A lot of our somedays are a way of postponing the beginning.
Near the end of his notebook, Marcus says the beginning has been available all along. Not after the next promotion or the next quiet season. Now, if you stop refusing it.

how: Readers who take this entry to heart often notice when they're postponing a good life until conditions change, and look for the part of it that's available today.

o: when what you hope for is already within reach
a hurried time to cram everything in before the end
the one day a year Romans set aside for rest

games.q: now, if you want it — tap the pairs.
p: set it toward reverence and justice

s: Marcus says the good life comes only after you've earned it
he says you can have it now, if you don't refuse it to yourself.
he writes that the thing to fear is not death but never beginning to live by nature
that's the sting at the end of the entry.

games.q: you're Marcus, near the end of your notebook. you've always thought you'd live well later, once things calm down. what does book twelve say?
o: you can have it now, if you stop refusing it.
games.why: leave the past, trust the future to providence, set the present right: then what you sought by a long road is yours now.

practice: Look for one good thing that's already here: the chair holding you, the breath moving, a person in the next room, a meal waiting, something you usually save until you've earned it. Don't earn it first.
Just receive it, fully, for this one minute.

wordCard.voice: Now. Marcus opens his last book: everything you hope to reach by a long road, you can have now, if you stop refusing it. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: now, not later. The life Marcus describes is already at your feet. Six hundred twenty-eight days, and counting.
